summary: Describes use cases and architecture for carrying PASSporT caller identity tokens outside the call signaling path, for calls that do not use SIP end-to-end or cannot deliver headers reliably.

plainLanguage.summary:
STIR is a way to prove who is calling. This RFC covers the calls where the proof cannot travel with the call, because the old telephone network is in the way.

The fix is a side route. The caller leaves a signed, encrypted token at a server under the called number. When the phone rings, the callee fetches that token and uses it to check the caller.

questions: how to verify caller identity without sip headers
what is a call placement service
how does out-of-band stir verify caller id
how does out-of-band stir deliver a passport
subtitle: How a caller's signed identity token reaches the callee by a side route when the telephone network cannot carry it.

tldr.problem: STIR proves who is calling, but many calls cross the legacy telephone network, which strips or damages the signed proof. The RFC describes where such calls come from and what the network cannot do.
tldr.mechanism: The caller or a gateway encrypts the PASSporT to the called party's public key and stores it at a Call Placement Service, indexed by the called number. When the call arrives, the callee fetches the token and decrypts it to check the calling number.
tldr.outcome: The RFC gives operating environments, five use cases, a broad architecture and a strawman HTTPS interface, but not a complete protocol. Any real deployment needs further specification.

facts.label: Encryption key used
facts.value: The called party's public encryption key

facts.label: CPS answer to any request
facts.value: At least one unique encrypted blob, even when idle

today: RFC 8816 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. The document is deliberately not a complete protocol: it describes the operating environments where out-of-band STIR is meant to work, gives use cases, a broad description of the components and a potential solution architecture, plus a strawman protocol for talking to the CPS. It says that deploying the framework in any particular environment would need additional specification outside the scope of the document.

sections.title: Why STIR Needs a Side Route
sections.content:
The STIR problem statement, RFC 7340, describes widespread problems enabled by impersonation in the telephone network: illegal robocalling, voicemail hacking and swatting. As telephone services move onto the Internet and use Voice over IP (VoIP) protocols such as SIP, those protocols need stronger identity mechanisms. RFC 8224 defines a SIP Identity header field that carries a PASSporT, a signed object attesting that the originator of a call is allowed to use the calling number.

Not every call uses SIP, and even those that do do not always carry SIP signalling end to end. Calls still routinely cross the Public Switched Telephone Network (PSTN). The RFC sorts calls into three groups: one or both ends is a PSTN endpoint; both ends are new-style but the call transits the PSTN somewhere; or the call never touches the PSTN at all. The first two groups are the majority, and they are where robocall problems live.

The PSTN's core devices are legacy equipment that is unlikely to be upgraded, so they cannot pass a signature through intact. Some would strip it from a signalling field; others would damage it past the point of verification. For those calls, no in-band authentication scheme looks practical today.

The endpoints, however, are becoming programmable: smart phones, IP private branch exchanges and terminal adapters are all general-purpose computers with both Internet and telephone access. That is what makes a side route possible.
sections.plainLanguage:
STIR attaches a signed proof of the caller's identity to a call. Many calls pass through the old telephone network, and that network cannot carry the proof without breaking it.

The way around this is to use the parts of the network that are now programmable, such as smart phones and IP-based phone systems, to pass the proof a different way.

sections.title: The Call Placement Service
sections.content:
Because the two ends cannot pass cryptographic information to each other through signalling, they need a rendezvous point. The RFC calls this a Call Placement Service (CPS): a service where a record of call placement, here a PASSporT, is stored for later retrieval. Minimally it holds a full-form PASSporT that names the caller, the callee and the time of the call.

The RFC describes two possible dataflows. In the first, the callee registers with the CPS and the CPS pushes the token to it, which needs a permanent connection from the callee and is awkward for mobile devices. The RFC dismisses this option: if the endpoints could hold such a connection, they could simply run a secure SIP session and carry the token in the call. So the second dataflow is used instead: the caller stores the token at the CPS when the call is placed, and the incoming call itself is the notification. The callee then asks the CPS for the tokens.

Nothing forces a particular operator. A CPS could run inside one network, be available publicly, be run by a carrier as a repository for its own customers, be built into an enterprise phone system, or even sit inside a single phone.

Discovery is not prescribed. The location of a CPS could be configured directly, recorded in the callee's credentials, looked up through a directory such as ENUM, or found through a distributed service such as RELOAD. The RFC notes that a single central CPS would have obvious scaling problems and would gather metadata about a very wide set of callers and callees, so any discovery mechanism should allow the CPS function to be federated.
sections.plainLanguage:
The two ends of the call cannot talk directly, so they need a meeting place. The RFC calls it a Call Placement Service, or CPS. The caller leaves a proof there, and the callee picks it up when the phone rings.

The RFC does not say who must run that server. It could sit inside one network, inside a phone system, or be offered to the public.

sections.title: Five Use Cases
sections.content:
The RFC walks through five situations. A call may carry more than one PASSporT, because a phone and the network it sits in can each create one for the same call.

  • VoIP to PSTN. The call starts in a STIR-aware SIP network, which creates a PASSporT and carries it in band. It then reaches a gateway to the PSTN. As a fallback, the authentication service also stores the token at the CPS under the target number. The smartphone that eventually rings asks the CPS and finds the token.
  • Two smart PSTN endpoints. An enterprise phone system with Internet access and a built-in gateway stores the token at the CPS before routing the call into the PSTN. The handset that rings queries the CPS and uses what it finds.
  • PSTN to VoIP. The enterprise phone system again stores the token. The call crosses the PSTN and arrives at an Internet gateway that turns it into SIP. Either that gateway retrieves the token and puts it in the new SIP request, or the verification service at the far end retrieves it.
  • Gateway out-of-band. The originating service does not support out-of-band delivery, so the gateway to the PSTN extracts the PASSporT from the SIP request and stores it at the CPS instead.
  • Enterprise call centre. A carrier creates a token and attaches it to a SIP call, and also stores it at the CPS as a fallback. The call later reaches a call centre over the PSTN, where a high-volume interface pulls tokens from the CPS so that agents can be shown a verified caller.
sections.plainLanguage:
The RFC lists five situations the design has to handle, from a call that starts on the Internet and ends on a mobile phone, to a call centre that receives calls over the old network.

In every case the same two moves happen: someone stores the proof at the CPS, and the party that receives the call fetches it.

sections.title: What the Two Services Do
sections.content:
The authentication service (AS) prepares the token in four steps. It first checks that it is authoritative for the identity it will put in the token's orig claim, which means it holds a matching private key, such as the key behind a STIR certificate. Second, it checks that the originator may claim that identity; for a service built into the calling device, this is the same key check. Third, it fetches the destination's public encryption key and discovers the CPS for that destination, collecting all public keys if there is more than one. Fourth, it creates the full-form PASSporT, sets the iat claim from the system time, fills in orig and dest, encrypts one copy per key found, and stores the result at the CPS. Only then is the call placed.

The verification service (VS) checks an arriving call in six steps. It asks the CPS for all current tokens for its number, or receives them over a push interface, and decrypts every one of them. Some will not decrypt: they may be meant for a different party, or they may be the dummy values the CPS invents for privacy. It then drops tokens with unsupported ppt extensions, keeps only those whose orig matches the calling number shown in signalling, drops those signed by credentials it does not trust, drops stale ones by checking the iat claim, and finally checks the signature over each remaining token.

What happens to a call that carries a valid token is left to local policy. The RFC notes that a call with no token is not necessarily bogus, because many legitimate calls will be unverifiable while the technology is being rolled out.
sections.plainLanguage:
The authentication service checks that it is allowed to speak for the calling number, encrypts a signed token for the called number and stores it. The verification service then fetches the tokens, decrypts them and checks each one in turn.

A call with no token is not automatically fake. Many genuine calls will lack one for a long time.

sections.title: Substitution Attacks and Flooding
sections.content:
The attack the design aims to stop is an attacker convincing the callee that a call comes from someone else. The RFC distinguishes two cases: impersonating a target when no call from that target is happening, and substituting the attacker into a call that is already being set up.

The substitution attack is the subtle one. A service that places automatic callbacks is the example. An attacker gives it the victim's number, so it stores a valid token and starts a call. At the same time the attacker places a call with forged caller ID that matches the callback service's number. If the attacker's call wins the race, the victim's phone verifies that call, because the two are indistinguishable, and the genuine callback goes to busy or voicemail.

The RFC notes that the window matters. The attack only works while the token sits at the CPS, so shortening that window makes it harder. It also notes that in SIP a callee might notice several requests, but in PSTN interworking only one setup attempt may reach the target.

Flooding is the second problem. If anyone may store tokens, an attacker can fill the CPS with millions of bogus ones under a given calling number, so the real token is buried. The proposed answer uses blind signatures. A client authenticates once and receives a signed token for a fresh key; later it stores a PASSporT anonymously, presenting that signed token, and the CPS can count how many times each token is used and refuse more. A CPS should also age tokens out, keeping them no longer than the sixty seconds that the iat freshness policy recommends, unless local policy says otherwise.
sections.plainLanguage:
The main risk is that an attacker races a fake call against a real one, so that the fake call is the one that gets verified. The risk lasts only as long as the token is stored, so a short storage window helps.

A second risk is flooding the server with fake tokens. The RFC's answer is to hand out signed tokens that limit how many entries one client may store.

sections.title: Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
Out-of-band delivery has different privacy properties from in-band STIR. In-band, the PASSporT travels as a cleartext header inside SIP messages, so any forwarding intermediary can inspect it. Out-of-band, the token is encrypted before it is stored and the CPS is the only intermediary, yet it cannot read what it holds.

Storing and retrieving tokens still leaks something. The RFC tries to limit this. A client need not authenticate to the CPS, which stops the CPS learning both the caller's and the callee's identity. The CPS must return at least one encrypted blob for every retrieval request, even when no call is in progress, and must never repeat a dummy blob, so that someone watching cannot tell a quiet number from a busy one. Authentication services may also store dummy tokens at random intervals, and a callee may request tokens for numbers it does not own, or for a whole range of numbers, to hide which numbers it controls.

The RFC also warns that a caller's IP address leaks information about the caller, and suggests proxying storage through a third party. It closes by saying the document only provides a framework, so the privacy properties of a real implementation depend on the environment it is deployed in. Closed systems may accept a weaker posture; open ones need the described practices.
sections.plainLanguage:
Keeping the proof off the signalling path can protect callers better, because the server that holds it cannot read it.

Some information still leaks. The server can see which numbers are called, and the caller's address is visible. The RFC asks servers to answer every request with something plausible, so that a quiet number looks like a busy one.
